After four hours, the fan container holds 92 milliliters and the still-air container 97 milliliters. No spills are observed. There is one trial per condition; water temperature and local humidity are not measured.
Report A: "The fan condition lost 8 milliliters, compared with 3 milliliters in still air. This is consistent with greater water loss near the fan in this trial."
Report B: "The fan caused exactly 8 milliliters of evaporation, and all open containers will lose this amount in four hours."
The record measures remaining volume, not the mechanism of every lost milliliter. The room, duration, starting amounts, and container type are supplied; generalization beyond them is untested. A simulation accompanying the reports assumes constant loss of 2 milliliters per hour near a fan. It predicts 92 milliliters after four hours and 84 after eight; the eight-hour result has not been observed.

explanation: A factual disagreement concerns incompatible claims about the same referent, such as 10:00 and 11:00 for one opening. An interpretive disagreement concerns what agreed facts mean, such as whether turnout counts as success. Locate the exact wording on each side before classifying the disagreement.

Apparent numerical conflict may arise from different definitions. Twenty-four signatures and twenty-eight entrants can both be correct because four people declined to sign. Do not average conflicting times to invent a compromise. Corroborating records support 10:00 here; 10:30 appears nowhere. Interpretation may remain open after a fact is resolved. A response can correct an inaccurate count and still acknowledge competing reasonable standards of success.

passages.title: Aesop’s race: traditional source
passages.text:
A Hare was one day making fun of a Tortoise for being so slow upon his feet. "Wait a bit," said the Tortoise; "I'll run a race with you, and I'll wager that I win." "Oh, well," replied the Hare, who was much amused at the idea, "let's try and see"; and it was soon agreed that the fox should set a course for them, and be the judge. When the time came both started off together, but the Hare was soon so far ahead that he thought he might as well have a rest: so down he lay and fell fast asleep.
Meanwhile the Tortoise kept plodding on, and in time reached the goal. At last the Hare woke up with a start, and dashed on at his fastest, but only to find that the Tortoise had already won the race.
passages.attribution: Traditional fable attributed to Aesop, The Hare and the Tortoise, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones in Aesop’s Fables (1912). Public domain in the United States; verified Project Gutenberg text.

passages.title: The route nobody won
passages.text:
[1] The neighborhood delivery contest offered a silver bicycle bell to the first team that brought a box of books to the hilltop reading room. Ren, who could sprint up the hill without stopping, named his team Hare. Suri named hers Tortoise because her borrowed cart had a stubborn wheel. "At least you understand the story," Ren said. "This time the hare will stay awake."
[2] The organizer marked a course from the square, over the footbridge, and up the hill. Each team received the same number of books. Ren raced ahead with his box while Suri tightened a loose cart strap. He did not rest. He crossed the bridge, climbed the first slope, and reached a fallen branch blocking the narrow path. He could step over it alone, but not while holding the wide box securely. He set the box down and tried to drag the branch. It would not move.
[3] Suri arrived slowly. Ren expected her to lift her books past him and continue. Instead, she wedged a flat stone beneath her cart wheel so it would not roll backward. "Your box could ride on my cart," she said. "Then both of us could move the branch." Ren looked at the silver bell drawn on the contest poster he had folded into his pocket. "Then which team wins?" Suri pulled at a smaller branch. "The room gets its books."
[4] Together they shifted the obstruction far enough to make a passage. They put both boxes on the cart and took turns steering it up the final slope. Ren's speed helped when they needed to carry books the last few steps; Suri's careful straps kept the remaining load in place. They reached the door together. The organizer held out the bell and asked whose team had crossed first.
[5] Ren began to answer, then put the folded poster on the desk. The edge was torn where the bell had been printed. "Can it go on the reading-room cart?" he asked. The organizer had a rule about first arrivals but none about shared ones. After a pause, she attached the bell to the cart. It made a thin sound, hardly a victory fanfare. Suri rang it again when the next delivery arrived, and Ren went down the steps to help unload.

Account B, newsletter written a week later: "The reading room opened at 11:00 and attracted twenty-four visitors before noon. The turnout was disappointing because forty people had registered interest."

passages.title: Learning through informal teachers

passages.title: Two interpretations of a container test
passages.text:
Invented experimental record. Two identical open containers begin with 100 milliliters of water each. One is placed by a fan and one in still air in the same room. After four hours, the fan container holds 92 milliliters and the still-air container 97 milliliters. No spills are observed. There is one trial per condition; water temperature and local humidity are not measured.
Report A: "The fan condition lost 8 milliliters, compared with 3 milliliters in still air. This is consistent with greater water loss near the fan in this trial."
Report B: "The fan caused exactly 8 milliliters of evaporation, and all open containers will lose this amount in four hours."
The record measures remaining volume, not the mechanism of every lost milliliter. The room, duration, starting amounts, and container type are supplied; generalization beyond them is untested. A simulation accompanying the reports assumes constant loss of 2 milliliters per hour near a fan. It predicts 92 milliliters after four hours and 84 after eight; the eight-hour result has not been observed.

After four hours, the fan container holds 92 milliliters and the still-air container 97 milliliters. No spills are observed. There is one trial per condition; water temperature and local humidity are not measured.
Report A: "The fan condition lost 8 milliliters, compared with 3 milliliters in still air. This is consistent with greater water loss near the fan in this trial."
Report B: "The fan caused exactly 8 milliliters of evaporation, and all open containers will lose this amount in four hours."
The record measures remaining volume, not the mechanism of every lost milliliter. The room, duration, starting amounts, and container type are supplied; generalization beyond them is untested. A simulation accompanying the reports assumes constant loss of 2 milliliters per hour near a fan. It predicts 92 milliliters after four hours and 84 after eight; the eight-hour result has not been observed.

No intermediate or later measurements exist, and the record does not identify the loss mechanism.

explanation: Use a four-part synthesis: shared evidence, explainable differences, unresolved contradictions, and interpretive choices. In the reading-room file, signatures and entrants are reconciled by definitions; opening times conflict; success judgments depend on benchmarks. passages.title: Aesop’s race: traditional source
passages.text:
A Hare was one day making fun of a Tortoise for being so slow upon his feet. "Wait a bit," said the Tortoise; "I'll run a race with you, and I'll wager that I win." "Oh, well," replied the Hare, who was much amused at the idea, "let's try and see"; and it was soon agreed that the fox should set a course for them, and be the judge. When the time came both started off together, but the Hare was soon so far ahead that he thought he might as well have a rest: so down he lay and fell fast asleep.
Meanwhile the Tortoise kept plodding on, and in time reached the goal. At last the Hare woke up with a start, and dashed on at his fastest, but only to find that the Tortoise had already won the race.
passages.attribution: Traditional fable attributed to Aesop, The Hare and the Tortoise, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones in Aesop’s Fables (1912). Public domain in the United States; verified Project Gutenberg text.

passages.title: The route nobody won
passages.text:
[1] The neighborhood delivery contest offered a silver bicycle bell to the first team that brought a box of books to the hilltop reading room. Ren, who could sprint up the hill without stopping, named his team Hare. Suri named hers Tortoise because her borrowed cart had a stubborn wheel. "At least you understand the story," Ren said. "This time the hare will stay awake."
[2] The organizer marked a course from the square, over the footbridge, and up the hill. Each team received the same number of books. Ren raced ahead with his box while Suri tightened a loose cart strap. He did not rest. He crossed the bridge, climbed the first slope, and reached a fallen branch blocking the narrow path. He could step over it alone, but not while holding the wide box securely. He set the box down and tried to drag the branch. It would not move.
[3] Suri arrived slowly. Ren expected her to lift her books past him and continue. Instead, she wedged a flat stone beneath her cart wheel so it would not roll backward. "Your box could ride on my cart," she said. "Then both of us could move the branch." Ren looked at the silver bell drawn on the contest poster he had folded into his pocket. "Then which team wins?" Suri pulled at a smaller branch. "The room gets its books."
[4] Together they shifted the obstruction far enough to make a passage. They put both boxes on the cart and took turns steering it up the final slope. Ren's speed helped when they needed to carry books the last few steps; Suri's careful straps kept the remaining load in place. They reached the door together. The organizer held out the bell and asked whose team had crossed first.
[5] Ren began to answer, then put the folded poster on the desk. The edge was torn where the bell had been printed. "Can it go on the reading-room cart?" he asked. The organizer had a rule about first arrivals but none about shared ones. After a pause, she attached the bell to the cart. It made a thin sound, hardly a victory fanfare. Suri rang it again when the next delivery arrived, and Ren went down the steps to help unload.

passages.title: Three accounts of a reading-room opening
passages.text:
Original civic source simulation; no real event is claimed.
Account A, organizer's note written on opening day: "We opened at 10:00. Twenty-four visitors signed the book by noon. Four others entered without signing, according to the door volunteer. The opening was a success because we exceeded our target of twenty visitors."
Account B, newsletter written a week later: "The reading room opened at 11:00 and attracted twenty-four visitors before noon. The turnout was disappointing because forty people had registered interest."
Account C, volunteer log: "Door opened 10:00. Signatures at 12:00: 24. Four people declined to sign. Interest list before opening: 40 names. No count was kept of how long visitors stayed."
Reading note: A and B disagree factually about the opening time. Their judgments also use different comparison standards: the organizer's target and the interest list. A signed count is not automatically a count of every entrant. C corroborates some statements but cannot establish whether every interested person intended to attend that morning.

passages.title: Learning through informal teachers
passages.text:
Frederick Douglass, first-person account from Chapter VII: "The plan which I adopted, and the one by which I was most successful, was that of making friends of all the little white boys whom I met in the street. As many of these as I could, I converted into teachers. With their kindly aid, obtained at different times and in different places, I finally succeeded in learning to read. When I was sent of errands, I always took my book with me, and by going one part of my errand quickly, I found time to get a lesson before my return."
Original secondary reading note written for Liminal: In this excerpt, Douglass describes arranging informal lessons while carrying out errands. The phrases "different times" and "different places" present a distributed learning process, not a single classroom session. He credits the boys' aid while also describing his own planning. The passage is part of his published narrative of enslavement; these selected sentences do not supply every stage of his learning or the later course of his life.
passages.attribution: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself (1845), Chapter VII, public domain in the United States. Verified Project Gutenberg transcription; clearly separated secondary note written for Liminal.

passages.title: The clock that waited
passages.text:
[1] I told everyone the station clock was useless after the trains stopped running. Why mend a thing whose appointments had disappeared? My aunt, who repaired watches at a narrow desk behind the ticket window, asked me to sweep the room instead of answering. Under the desk I found the envelope she had sent to the council three months earlier: an estimate for repairing the clock, returned with a note that funding was postponed.
[2] I had tried to repair it myself before that letter came back. I could clean the face and reset the hands, but the mechanism stopped again within an hour. When Aunt asked what I had learned, I said that nobody looked at it anyway. She put my tools away one by one. "That wasn't what I asked."
[3] The next Saturday, a walking group waited beneath the tower. Their printed route said, "Meet under the station clock at nine." One person checked a wristwatch, another a phone. The tower hands remained at six seventeen. The group still found one another. I almost took this as proof that the clock did not matter. Then a child asked why the tower was allowed to tell the same wrong story all day.
[4] I went back inside. Aunt had spread the council letter beside a diagram of the mechanism. "We can clean what we understand," she said. "For the rest, we need someone who knows more." I wanted her to say the clock was beyond repair. Instead, she asked me to list the parts I could name. The list was short. Below it I wrote the question I had avoided: Why does it stop?
[5] We made an exhibition in the ticket room. We displayed the clock's working drawing, the unanswered question, and a recording of its uneven tick from my failed attempt. I labeled the recording "trial, not repair." A retired mechanic left a note offering to inspect the mechanism, without promising to fix it. The council still had not approved funds. Nothing in the tower moved.

passages.title: The clock that waited
passages.text:
[1] I told everyone the station clock was useless after the trains stopped running. Why mend a thing whose appointments had disappeared? My aunt, who repaired watches at a narrow desk behind the ticket window, asked me to sweep the room instead of answering. Under the desk I found the envelope she had sent to the council three months earlier: an estimate for repairing the clock, returned with a note that funding was postponed.
[2] I had tried to repair it myself before that letter came back. I could clean the face and reset the hands, but the mechanism stopped again within an hour. When Aunt asked what I had learned, I said that nobody looked at it anyway. She put my tools away one by one. "That wasn't what I asked."
[3] The next Saturday, a walking group waited beneath the tower. Their printed route said, "Meet under the station clock at nine." One person checked a wristwatch, another a phone. The tower hands remained at six seventeen. The group still found one another. I almost took this as proof that the clock did not matter. Then a child asked why the tower was allowed to tell the same wrong story all day.
[4] I went back inside. Aunt had spread the council letter beside a diagram of the mechanism. "We can clean what we understand," she said. "For the rest, we need someone who knows more." I wanted her to say the clock was beyond repair. Instead, she asked me to list the parts I could name. The list was short. Below it I wrote the question I had avoided: Why does it stop?
[5] We made an exhibition in the ticket room. We displayed the clock's working drawing, the unanswered question, and a recording of its uneven tick from my failed attempt. I labeled the recording "trial, not repair." A retired mechanic left a note offering to inspect the mechanism, without promising to fix it. The council still had not approved funds. Nothing in the tower moved.
[6] On the following Saturday, I met the walking group at six seventeen by the tower and nine by my wristwatch. I showed the child the diagram through the window. "It isn't useless," I said. "It isn't working either." She studied both the clock and my watch, as though each might explain the other. When Aunt opened the room, I carried in a chair for the mechanic and left the tools on the desk.

passages.title: The clock that waited
passages.text:
[1] I told everyone the station clock was useless after the trains stopped running. Why mend a thing whose appointments had disappeared? My aunt, who repaired watches at a narrow desk behind the ticket window, asked me to sweep the room instead of answering. Under the desk I found the envelope she had sent to the council three months earlier: an estimate for repairing the clock, returned with a note that funding was postponed.
[2] I had tried to repair it myself before that letter came back. I could clean the face and reset the hands, but the mechanism stopped again within an hour. When Aunt asked what I had learned, I said that nobody looked at it anyway. She put my tools away one by one. "That wasn't what I asked."
[3] The next Saturday, a walking group waited beneath the tower. Their printed route said, "Meet under the station clock at nine." One person checked a wristwatch, another a phone. The tower hands remained at six seventeen. The group still found one another. I almost took this as proof that the clock did not matter. Then a child asked why the tower was allowed to tell the same wrong story all day.
[4] I went back inside. Aunt had spread the council letter beside a diagram of the mechanism. "We can clean what we understand," she said. "For the rest, we need someone who knows more." I wanted her to say the clock was beyond repair. Instead, she asked me to list the parts I could name. The list was short. Below it I wrote the question I had avoided: Why does it stop?
[5] We made an exhibition in the ticket room. We displayed the clock's working drawing, the unanswered question, and a recording of its uneven tick from my failed attempt. I labeled the recording "trial, not repair." A retired mechanic left a note offering to inspect the mechanism, without promising to fix it. The council still had not approved funds. Nothing in the tower moved.
[6] On the following Saturday, I met the walking group at six seventeen by the tower and nine by my wristwatch. I showed the child the diagram through the window. "It isn't useless," I said. "It isn't working either." She studied both the clock and my watch, as though each might explain the other. When Aunt opened the room, I carried in a chair for the mechanic and left the tools on the desk.

passages.title: The clock that waited
passages.text:
[1] I told everyone the station clock was useless after the trains stopped running. Why mend a thing whose appointments had disappeared? My aunt, who repaired watches at a narrow desk behind the ticket window, asked me to sweep the room instead of answering. Under the desk I found the envelope she had sent to the council three months earlier: an estimate for repairing the clock, returned with a note that funding was postponed.
[2] I had tried to repair it myself before that letter came back. I could clean the face and reset the hands, but the mechanism stopped again within an hour. When Aunt asked what I had learned, I said that nobody looked at it anyway. She put my tools away one by one. "That wasn't what I asked."
[3] The next Saturday, a walking group waited beneath the tower. Their printed route said, "Meet under the station clock at nine." One person checked a wristwatch, another a phone. The tower hands remained at six seventeen. The group still found one another. I almost took this as proof that the clock did not matter. Then a child asked why the tower was allowed to tell the same wrong story all day.
[4] I went back inside. Aunt had spread the council letter beside a diagram of the mechanism. "We can clean what we understand," she said. "For the rest, we need someone who knows more." I wanted her to say the clock was beyond repair. Instead, she asked me to list the parts I could name. The list was short. Below it I wrote the question I had avoided: Why does it stop?
[5] We made an exhibition in the ticket room. We displayed the clock's working drawing, the unanswered question, and a recording of its uneven tick from my failed attempt. I labeled the recording "trial, not repair." A retired mechanic left a note offering to inspect the mechanism, without promising to fix it. The council still had not approved funds. Nothing in the tower moved.
[6] On the following Saturday, I met the walking group at six seventeen by the tower and nine by my wristwatch. I showed the child the diagram through the window. "It isn't useless," I said. "It isn't working either." She studied both the clock and my watch, as though each might explain the other. When Aunt opened the room, I carried in a chair for the mechanic and left the tools on the desk.

passages.title: Douglass on bread, knowledge, and naming helpers
passages.text:
Frederick Douglass, Chapter VII, consecutive excerpt: "I used also to carry bread with me, enough of which was always in the house, and to which I was always welcome; for I was much better off in this regard than many of the poor white children in our neighborhood. This bread I used to bestow upon the hungry little urchins, who, in return, would give me that more valuable bread of knowledge.
I am strongly tempted to give the names of two or three of those little boys, as a testimonial of the gratitude and affection I bear them; but prudence forbids;—not that it would injure me, but it might embarrass them; for it is almost an unpardonable offence to teach slaves to read in this Christian country. It is enough to say of the dear little fellows, that they lived on Philpot Street, very near Durgin and Bailey's ship-yard. I used to talk this matter of slavery over with them."
Original editorial context: Douglass's published narrative recounts his life under enslavement. This selection follows his description of arranging informal reading lessons with boys he met. It presents both exchange and the narrator's later decision about naming helpers. The excerpt's judgment about teaching reflects his condemnation of the society described; it is not the instructional author's endorsement of restrictions on literacy.
passages.attribution: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself (1845), Chapter VII, public-domain text in the United States, verified at Project Gutenberg. Apostrophe style normalized; editorial context written for Liminal.

passages.title: Two readings of a remembered exchange
passages.text:
Original secondary commentary on the supplied Douglass excerpt.
Reading A: The exchange is reciprocal: Douglass supplies food to hungry children, and they supply instruction. The phrase "more valuable bread of knowledge" shows that he values learning beyond the physical bread he gives. His account does not erase the children's material need, nor does having bread make him free. The comparison is local: he says he was better supplied "in this regard."
Reading B: The passage is chiefly about the responsibility of a narrator. Douglass wants to name the boys in gratitude but withholds their names because of possible consequences for them. By naming a street and a nearby shipyard, he provides setting without providing their individual identities. The reader learns that omission can be deliberate protection rather than mere forgetfulness.
Synthesis note: A and B emphasize different aspects without directly contradicting each other. Neither claims access to the boys' private thoughts. A full historical interpretation would require more of the narrative and other contextual sources; this selected passage supports a focused analysis of exchange, valuation, and protective disclosure.

passages.title: Timing record, graph description, and report
passages.text:
Invented technical investigation. A mechanical timer is compared with a reference stopwatch. At reference times 0, 5, 10, and 15 minutes, the timer displays 0, 4.8, 9.6, and 14.4 minutes. The supplied graph has reference minutes on the horizontal axis from 0 to 15 and timer minutes on the vertical axis from 0 to 15. Plot the four ordered pairs (0,0), (5,4.8), (10,9.6), and (15,14.4). They lie on a straight line below the equal-reading line y = x, except at the origin.
Report A: "At the three nonzero observations, the timer displayed 96 percent of the reference elapsed time. It lagged by 0.6 minute at the 15-minute observation."
Report B: "The timer loses 0.6 minute every minute and will always follow the same pattern." The record contains only these observations in one trial; it supplies no cause, uncertainty estimate, or later measurements. A model assumes y = 0.96x and predicts a timer display of 28.8 minutes when the reference reaches 30. That prediction has not been observed.

passages.title: Two treatments of the clock scene

Treatment B: Show the narrator saying the clock is useless, then immediately show a montage of polishing gears. End with the clock striking nine as everyone applauds. Omit the council letter, the failed trial label, and the unanswered question.

Original editorial context: Douglass's published narrative recounts his life under enslavement. This selection follows his description of arranging informal reading lessons with boys he met. It presents both exchange and the narrator's later decision about naming helpers. The excerpt's judgment about teaching reflects his condemnation of the society described; it is not the instructional author's endorsement of restrictions on literacy.

passages.title: Two readings of a remembered exchange
passages.text:
Original secondary commentary on the supplied Douglass excerpt.
Reading A: The exchange is reciprocal: Douglass supplies food to hungry children, and they supply instruction. The phrase "more valuable bread of knowledge" shows that he values learning beyond the physical bread he gives. His account does not erase the children's material need, nor does having bread make him free. The comparison is local: he says he was better supplied "in this regard."
Reading B: The passage is chiefly about the responsibility of a narrator. Douglass wants to name the boys in gratitude but withholds their names because of possible consequences for them. By naming a street and a nearby shipyard, he provides setting without providing their individual identities. The reader learns that omission can be deliberate protection rather than mere forgetfulness.
Synthesis note: A and B emphasize different aspects without directly contradicting each other. Neither claims access to the boys' private thoughts. A full historical interpretation would require more of the narrative and other contextual sources; this selected passage supports a focused analysis of exchange, valuation, and protective disclosure.

passages.title: Timing record, graph description, and report
passages.text:
Invented technical investigation. A mechanical timer is compared with a reference stopwatch. At reference times 0, 5, 10, and 15 minutes, the timer displays 0, 4.8, 9.6, and 14.4 minutes. The supplied graph has reference minutes on the horizontal axis from 0 to 15 and timer minutes on the vertical axis from 0 to 15. Plot the four ordered pairs (0,0), (5,4.8), (10,9.6), and (15,14.4). They lie on a straight line below the equal-reading line y = x, except at the origin.
Report A: "At the three nonzero observations, the timer displayed 96 percent of the reference elapsed time. It lagged by 0.6 minute at the 15-minute observation."
Report B: "The timer loses 0.6 minute every minute and will always follow the same pattern." The record contains only these observations in one trial; it supplies no cause, uncertainty estimate, or later measurements. A model assumes y = 0.96x and predicts a timer display of 28.8 minutes when the reference reaches 30. That prediction has not been observed.

passages.title: Two treatments of the clock scene
passages.text:
Original described adaptation plans; no actual film is supplied.
Treatment A: Begin with a close view of motionless hands at six seventeen. Play the uneven tick recording while showing the label "trial, not repair." End on the narrator placing a chair for the mechanic beside the still clock; use no triumphant music.
Treatment B: Show the narrator saying the clock is useless, then immediately show a montage of polishing gears. End with the clock striking nine as everyone applauds. Omit the council letter, the failed trial label, and the unanswered question.
Both are proposals for adapting the supplied fiction. A designer's predicted audience effect is an interpretation of these choices, not evidence from an audience study.

passages.title: The community exhibit dossier
passages.text: Original final source set. Story: Eda calls an old camera worthless after failing to develop its film. Later she labels her trial "image unresolved" and asks an experienced photographer for help. Civic record: an exhibit log lists 30 entrants, including 5 volunteers; a poster says "30 independent visitors learned photography." Technical record: a demonstration timer shows 7.6 minutes when a reference shows 8; a model assumes display = 0.95 × reference and predicts 19 at reference time 20. Commentary: the exhibit was worthwhile because it prompted questions. No learning assessment, later timer measurement, or successful film result is supplied.
